newsitem.title: CHINA: Siam Cement, TPI, Thai Airways seen weak - Merrill.
newsitem.headline: Siam Cement, TPI, Thai Airways seen weak - Merrill.

text.p: Siam Cement Co Plc, TPI Polene Co Ltd and Sahaviriya Steel Industries Plc are among Thai companies expected to suffer the most from a weaker baht, according to Merrill Lynch.
Thai Airways International Ltd, which has big foreign borrowings, would also be a victim.
But Thai banks and finance companies should escape the worst damage from a weaker baht because of government regulations restricting their foreign borrowings, Merrill Lynch said.

Being one of Thailand's largest private sector borrowers of foreign currency loans, Siam Cement is expected to suffer a lot of damage to its bottom line although its cash flow should remain protected, the brokerage said.

Siam Cement is one of Thailand's largest private sector borrowers of foreign currency loans, with an unhedged exposure of US$3.7 billion. If losses from a 10 percent baht depreciation were factored in immediately, an estimated 1997 net profit of 7.2 billion baht would turn to a net loss of 1.4 billion. But company cash flow would fall by only 17 percent.

"We concede that a sharply weaker baht could damage Siam Cement's balance sheet quite severely and put pressure on the company to raise capital," Merrill Lynch said. "However, we believe its impeccable shareholder structure ... excellent credit standing, and professional management should ensure continuing support from creditor banks."

TPI Polene would also be significantly damaged by a weaker baht, with unhedged foreign currency debts of US$1.3 billion comprising short-term debt of US$500 million, long-term loans of US$600 million and debentures of US$205 million, Merrill Lynch said.
A 10-percent baht depreciation would turn estimated 1997 net income to a loss and cash flow would drop by 46 percent.
"We remain concerned about the company's deteriorating financial position and believe that continuing support from its offshore creditors will be critical," the brokerage said.
Thai Airways is also considered a victim, with 46 percent of its revenue in U.S. dollars and U.S. dollar costs amounting to roughly 50 percent of operating costs.
Up to 93.3 percent of the airline's borrowings are foreign currency denominated, with approximately 64 percent of the airline's 80.8 billion baht debt in U.S. dollars.
"Should Thai decide to write off the exchange losses all at once, the airline would immediately plunge into a substantial net loss," Merrill Lynch said.

In the construction sector, Shaviriya Steel Industry "could suffer a serious setback from a weaker baht". It has outstanding unhedged U.S. dollar loans of US$242 million, comprising short-term loans of US$100 million, long-term loans of US$37 million and a Euroconvertible of US$105 million due in 2005.

PTT Exploration and Production plc offers one of the best hedges against a weaker baht because not only are the company's gas, oil and condensate commodity prices directly linked to the U.S. dollar, but so are a large proportion of its earnings, Merrill Lynch noted.
In the banking sector, commercial banks' naked foreign exchange exposure is limited to 15 percent of their capital funds, which suggests the impact of a baht depreciation is likely to be moderate.
Assuming a 10 percent baht depreciation, the banks' 1997 net earnings estimate would fall by six percent. A 20 percent depreciation would lead to a 12-15 percent drop in earnings.
Merrill's preferred stocks are Bangkok Bank Plc, Thai Farmers Bank Ltd and Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand.
Maximum foreign exposure for finance companies is 20 percent of shareholders' funds.

"With other developments, such as portfolio losses, the SET (Stock Exchange of Thailand) slump and a hike in provisions against non-performing loans, already causing intermediate term distortions to earnings, the impact of translation losses would be minimal to the finance companies' 1997 earnings per share estimates," Merrill said.
Sector favorite is National Finance and Securities plc, which has disclosed that it is only exposed to a US$64.5 million position hedged to a baht exchange rate of 28.1 per U.S. dollar.
Phatra Thanakit Co Ltd is fully hedged. Dhana Siam Finance and Securities Plc and Asia Credit Ltd have exposure of less than 12 percent of shareholders' funds in the period prior to June.
